issues.legal_issue: A profit from an isolated purchase and resale of property is business income when the transaction, considered as a whole, has essential features of trade.
material_facts: A firm whose ordinary business did not include investing in land acquired adjoining plots over a period of time and later sold them to a company it managed for substantially more than their purchase price.
The fact-finder found that the plots were acquired solely to resell them to the company at a profit, and rejected explanations that they were acquired as an investment or to provide housing.

The firm did not cultivate or develop the plots or otherwise use them; the surrounding circumstances supported the finding that the acquisitions formed a profit-making scheme, and no relevant circumstances offset the presumption arising from the sole resale intention.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was an adventure in the nature of trade, and the resulting profit was properly assessed as business income.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(4) and 10 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, an isolated transaction may be an adventure in the nature of trade if it has some essential features of trade or business. The character of a transaction depends on the total effect of all relevant circumstances, not a mechanical count of factors. A sole and exclusive intention to resell at a profit, coupled with no intention to hold, enjoy, or use the property, raises a strong but rebuttable presumption of an adventure in the nature of trade. The Court considered, among other authorities, The Californian Copper Syndicate v. Harris, Commissioner of Inland Revenue v. Livingston, Rutledge v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Balgownie Land Trust Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Martin v. Lowry, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Fraser, and Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Reinhold.

predicates.income_tax_business_income_classificatio: The dispute concerns whether profit from a transaction is taxable as income from a business.
predicates.isolated_property_purchase_resale: A person acquired property in an isolated transaction and later resold it.
predicates.sole_resale_profit_intent: The fact-finder found that the person acquired the property solely to resell it at a profit.
predicates.no_intention_to_hold_or_use: The person had no intention of retaining, enjoying, or using the property.

predicates.no_countervailing_factors_rebut_presumpt: The other relevant circumstances did not rebut the presumption arising from the sole intention to resell at a profit.

issues.definition: When a business-income classification concerns an isolated property purchase and resale, and the sole resale intention, lack of intent to hold or use, and profit-making scheme are not counterbalanced by other circumstances, the profit is treated as business income.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a transaction is an adventure in the nature of trade is a mixed question of law and fact reviewable in a statutory income-tax reference.
material_facts: The fact-finder made findings about the acquisitions, the intended resale, the use of the property, and the circumstances of the sale.
The reference challenged whether those facts justified treating the transaction as an adventure in the nature of trade.
Deciding that characterization required applying the legal meaning of trade to the primary facts.
issues.conclusion: The transaction’s characterization was a mixed question of law and fact and could be examined in the reference; the appropriate inquiry was whether the inference of an adventure in the nature of trade was justified in law on the proved facts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 66(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, permits consideration of questions of law in a reference. Under Meenakshi Mills, Madurai v. Commissioner of Income-tax and Oriental Investment Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, the legal effect of facts and the correct application of legal principles may raise a question of law even where primary factual findings are accepted. The Court considered Edwards v. Bairstow and held it consistent with treating the characterization of a transaction as a mixed question of law and fact.
